tldr: By identifying stable contact locations on the object's surface from monocular videos and using them to guide both reconstruction and retargeting to a robot hand, this study achieves high-precision dexterous manipulation free from contact slippage and penetration.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of the proposed method, C2Dex. From a monocular video, stable contact points are extracted in the canonical object space to optimize human hand-object interaction trajectories (top), which are then transferred into executable robot trajectories via Laplacian geometry preservation and residual reinforcement learning (bottom).
overview:
Teaching complex tasks to dexterous robot hands requires high-quality data with aligned motions of hands, objects, and contacts. However, collecting such data via teleoperation or motion capture demands dedicated equipment and is difficult to scale. Therefore, extracting motions from everyday monocular human videos and transferring them to robots has attracted significant attention.

However, 3D hand-object interaction (HOI) reconstruction from monocular videos often suffers from frame-wise contact jitter and hand-object penetration due to occlusions and depth ambiguity. Furthermore, because human and robot hands differ in finger counts and link lengths, merely matching joint angles breaks essential contact points and local spatial relationships.

This paper presents "C2Dex", which solves this issue with the idea of "aggregating stable object-side contacts in the canonical object space (the object's local coordinate frame) as a shared beacon." By first identifying temporally stable contact points on the object surface, it reconstructs jitter-free human hand trajectories under these contact constraints. Then, during retargeting to the robot hand, an optimization preserves these contact goals while maintaining the local geometric structure between the hand and object.

In experiments on standard benchmarks (DexYCB and TACO), C2Dex achieved end-to-end trajectory success rates of 57.78% and 26.67%, overwhelmingly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines at 17.78% and 10.00%. On a real robot (Unitree G1 with Inspire dexterous hands), it also stably reproduced 8 contact-rich manipulation tasks.
contributions: Proposed an interaction representation that aggregates noisy frame-wise contact estimates across time in the canonical object space to identify stable object-side contact points.

Constructed a temporally coherent human hand-object trajectory reconstruction method that leverages these stable contacts as trajectory-level constraints to prevent contact separation and penetration.
Developed a retargeting method combining stable contact tracking with Laplacian optimization to preserve local hand-object geometry across different embodiments.
Built an end-to-end system from video to simulation and a real humanoid robot, substantially improving the success rate of dexterous object manipulation.

sections.heading: Dexterous Robot Control from Monocular Video: How to Stop Contact Jitter?
sections.summary: Collecting dexterous demonstrations is costly, while monocular videos offer abundant and diverse behaviors. However, monocular contact reconstruction is vulnerable to noise, and embodiment differences cause contacts to fail. C2Dex resolves these issues by using stable contacts on the object surface as a shared reference.
sections.details:
Learning dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands requires joint angles, object motions, and the exact evolution of where and how contacts occur. However, gathering such data via teleoperation or motion capture requires expensive setups and immense human effort. In contrast, monocular videos captured with smartphones are ubiquitous on the web, offering a treasure trove of diverse manipulation behaviors.

Nevertheless, two major hurdles stand in the way of turning videos into executable robot trajectories. First, monocular hand-object interaction (HOI) reconstruction is severely challenged by occlusions and depth ambiguity, leading to fingertip jitter and penetration into objects. Second, even with a clean human trajectory, robot hands have different kinematic configurations and finger lengths. Simply mimicking fingertip positions or joint angles easily loses the contacts critical for the task.

At the root of both problems is the lack of a temporally stable description of where contacts occur on the object. C2Dex addresses this by transforming noisy frame-wise contact estimates into the object's local coordinates (canonical object space) to extract stable contacts anchored to the object. Using these as shared constraints in both reconstruction and retargeting modules ensures consistent contacts all the way from video to real-world execution.

sections.heading: At the Intersection of Monocular Reconstruction and Robot Retargeting
sections.summary: Existing monocular HOI methods often operate frame-by-frame, causing temporal contact drift. Meanwhile, existing retargeting methods focus heavily on hand-alone similarity, disrupting interactions with objects. C2Dex bridges this gap by focusing on object-side contacts and local geometry preservation.
sections.details:
This work intersects three main areas of research:

- Hand-Object Reconstruction from Monocular Video (HOI Reconstruction):
Recent approaches leverage template-free methods, diffusion models, and geometric priors for robust reconstruction. However, they frequently process frames independently. Even if the visual pose looks plausible, contact locations drift over time. While acceptable for human-viewed CG animations, this is fatal for physics-bound robot manipulation. C2Dex aggregates contact evidence across frames in the canonical object space to achieve physically plausible stability.

- Retargeting to Dexterous Hands:
Existing techniques track fingertip positions, map joint angles, or learn geometric correspondences. However, they focus primarily on "how to make the hand pose look similar." By matching hand poses in isolation without considering the object, small errors in the input trajectory are amplified, causing severe penetrations or broken contacts. In contrast, C2Dex explicitly preserves the relative spatial structure between hand and object using Laplacian mesh coordinates.

- Dexterous Manipulation Learning from Video:
Most prior methods assumed the availability of clean motion capture data to drive reinforcement learning (RL). Recent attempts try learning directly from video, but their success rates remain low due to upstream visual perception errors. C2Dex tackles these perceptual errors at the root through contact consistency.

sections.heading: Aggregating Contacts in Object Space and Preserving Geometry on Robots
sections.summary: The method first estimates initial hand and object trajectories, then clusters contact points in the canonical object space to obtain stable contacts. These contacts guide penetration-free human trajectory optimization, followed by Laplacian optimization and residual reinforcement learning to produce physically executable robot trajectories.
sections.details:
C2Dex consists of two tightly coupled stages: Contact-Consistent HOI Reconstruction and Contact-Interaction-Preserving Retargeting.

### III-A Contact-Consistent HOI Reconstruction
- Initial Hand and Object Estimation:
Frame-wise MANO hand joint angles $\boldsymbol{\theta}^0_t$ and global poses $\boldsymbol{\tau}^0_t$ are estimated using Dyn-HaMR. For the object, SAM 3D reconstructs a 3D mesh, and ProxyPose estimates the 6-DoF poses $(\mathbf{R}_{o,t}, \mathbf{p}_{o,t})$.

- Temporal Contact Stabilization:
Candidate vertices are detected in 2D silhouette overlap regions, and camera rays are cast to find intersections $\mathbf{x}_{t,i}$ with the object surface. These points are filtered based on opposing surface normals between hand and object (negative dot product exceeding a threshold). Crucially, these contact points are transformed into the canonical object space using the inverse of the object pose. Once rigid object motion is canceled out, contacts are clustered across temporal segments with small joint variations using DBSCAN. The medoid of the largest cluster is designated as the true stable contact point for that segment.

- Trajectory Optimization:
The entire human hand trajectory is re-optimized using a contact loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{contact}}^h$ pulling hand vertices toward the stable contacts, a penetration loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pene}}^h$ penalizing intersections using the object's Signed Distance Function (SDF), and smoothness regularizers. This yields clean human trajectories free of slip and penetration.

### III-B Contact-Interaction-Preserving Retargeting
- Stable Contact Tracking and Laplacian Interaction Optimization:
To transfer motions from the human hand to the robot hand, keypoint-based matching first provides a rough pose. Next, a contact loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{contact}}^{\mathrm{ret}}$ aligns the robot fingertip contacts $\mathbf{y}^d_{t,f}$ with the stable contacts recovered on the object. Furthermore, to maintain the local spatial arrangement, a 3D Delaunay graph is constructed connecting hand keypoints and sampled object points. The Laplacian coordinates (relative vectors to neighbors) of each vertex are computed, and an optimization loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Lap}}^{\mathrm{ret}}$ enforces that the robot hand and object preserve these same relative relationships. Because it preserves local geometry rather than absolute coordinates, the transfer succeeds despite differing hand scales and kinematics.

- Refinement via Residual Reinforcement Learning:
Following trajectory optimization with joint limit constraints and SDF collision avoidance, a residual reinforcement learning policy (PPO) is trained in Isaac Gym simulation. It fine-tunes minor dynamical discrepancies arising in the simulator to output the final executable trajectory. This policy is used solely to refine trajectories; real-robot deployment operates purely via open-loop trajectory replay.

sections.heading: Tripling Trajectory Success Rates and Operating Stably on a Humanoid
sections.summary: Evaluated on DexYCB and TACO benchmarks, C2Dex dramatically outperformed prior methods in end-to-end trajectory success rates. It also set the best scores in physical stability of reconstruction and low retargeting penetration, successfully replaying 8 tasks on a real Unitree G1 humanoid robot.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted on DexYCB (45 sequences) and TACO (30 sequences). In end-to-end trajectory generation, success is determined by the object's Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE) in simulation, requiring position error $\le 0.10\text{ m}$ and rotation error $\le 1.00\text{ rad}$ (relaxed) or $\le 0.50\text{ rad}$ (strict). Baselines included state-of-the-art video-based methods: Do As I Do and DexImit.

### End-to-End Trajectory Generation Results
On DexYCB, while the strongest baseline achieved a success rate of 17.78% (17.78% strict), C2Dex reached 57.78% (55.56% strict). On the more challenging TACO dataset, C2Dex achieved 26.67% (23.33% strict) compared to the baseline's 10.00%. A drastic drop in failed drops due to lost contacts accounted for this large margin.

### Quality of HOI Reconstruction
To measure physical plausibility, Simulation Displacement (SD)—the distance an object moved over 1,000 steps in physics simulation—was evaluated. While the best baseline moved by 4.55 cm, C2Dex drifted by only 1.57 cm, confirming proper hand-object fit without unintended repulsive forces or slipping.

### Retargeting Accuracy
Using ground-truth human trajectories as input, retargeting to the Inspire Hand showed contact position error dropping from 16.51 mm to 11.87 mm, normal alignment error halving from 34.92 degrees to 18.13 degrees, and maximum penetration depth plummeting from 22.92 mm to just 3.99 mm.

### Ablation Studies
Removing contact consistency (CC) and reverting to frame-wise contacts caused the DexYCB success rate to collapse from 57.78% to 17.78%. Removing the Laplacian loss also led to a substantial drop, proving that canonical contact aggregation and hand-object geometry preservation are both indispensable.

### Real-Robot Experiments
Using a Unitree G1 humanoid equipped with Inspire dexterous hands, 8 contact-rich manipulation tasks (totaling 24 demonstration videos)—including hat hanging, sweeping debris, wiping a whiteboard, and bin trash disposal—were executed in an open-loop replay. Simply placing the object at the video's initial location allowed the robot to reliably reproduce the grasping and wiping behaviors.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Outlook: The Power of Contact-Centric Video Imitation
sections.summary: C2Dex paves the way for reliable motion transfer from monocular video to dexterous hands through contact consistency and geometric preservation. Current limitations include extreme occlusions, object pose drift, and lack of support for finger gating, pointing to promising avenues for future research.
sections.details:
This paper presented C2Dex, a novel framework for generating dexterous manipulation trajectories from monocular videos. Its core design philosophy is straightforward: identify stable contacts in the canonical object space and use them consistently from reconstruction through retargeting. Comprehensive benchmark evaluations and real-robot trials strongly validated the effectiveness of this contact-preserving approach.

At the same time, the authors transparently note several limitations:
- Under severe occlusions, extreme camera viewpoints, or complex object geometries, extracting initial interaction cues can fail.
- The method relies on accurate 6-DoF object pose estimation; tracking errors disrupt canonical contact aggregation.
- The current formulation assumes stable contact phases over temporal windows and does not support complex in-hand manipulation with continuous contact switching, such as finger gaiting.

Future work aims to enhance visual robustness under challenging conditions and expand the framework toward advanced manipulation involving continuous in-hand contact transitions.

takeaways: Frame-wise jitter and contact drift—the biggest hurdles in monocular HOI reconstruction—can be dramatically mitigated by aggregating contacts temporally in the object's canonical local space.

When retargeting to robot hands with different kinematics, preserving object-surface contacts and local hand-object geometry (Laplacian coordinates) is far more effective than tracking joint angles or absolute positions.

Using residual reinforcement learning strictly for final physical trajectory refinement in simulation enables high-fidelity open-loop execution on real hardware without needing real-time visual policies.
limitations: Heavily relies on the quality of initial 3D object reconstruction and frame-wise 6-DoF pose tracking; failures in object tracking cascade into failed contact aggregation.
Assumes locally stable contact phases, making it unable to handle in-hand manipulation with frequent contact switching, such as pen spinning or finger gaiting.

Real-robot deployment relies on an open-loop replay protocol where humans manually align the object's initial pose to the video, lacking closed-loop visual feedback against environmental disturbances.
